stimulus.text:
“Grant that their minds are by nature equal, yet who shall wonder at the apparent superiority, if indeed custom becomes second nature; nay if it taketh place of nature, and that it doth the experience of each day will evince. . . . May we not trace its source in the difference of education, and in the difference of the objects to which the attention of the two sexes is directed?”
— Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March–April 1790 (written 1779; abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes,” Massachusetts Magazine, March-April 1790. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Judith Sargent Murray, “On the Equality of the Sexes” (1790), public domain.

stem: Murray's essay most directly calls for women to receive

options.text: The same serious education as men
The right to vote for members of Congress
options.misconception: The vote never appears in the passage; Murray asks about minds and education, not the ballot.

options.text: Equal pay for equal work in shops and farms
options.misconception: Pay never appears in the passage; her subject is education and the mind, not wages.

options.text: The right to hold public office in the new republic
options.misconception: Officeholding never appears in the passage; Murray asks for serious studies, not for public office.

rationales.A: Murray traces women's apparent inferiority to the difference of education, so her remedy is the same serious studies for women that men receive.
rationales.B: Voting is not her ask; the passage argues about education, not the ballot.
rationales.C: Wages are not her subject; the passage is about minds, custom, and schooling.
rationales.D: Office is not her ask; she wants women's minds taken seriously through education.
rationales.general:
1. Find the cause she names. The difference of education between the sexes.
2. Find the remedy that fits. The same serious education for women as for men.
3. Rule out the rest. No vote, no wages, and no office appear anywhere in the passage.
Remember: a remedy must fit the cause the author names — match the answer to her own diagnosis.
